paper_title: Agent World Model in the Wild: Computer-Use Agent Environment Synthesis

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Agent learning is shifting from learning from human data toward learning through interaction with the world. However, scaling such learning directly in real-world computer systems is challenging and can introduce substantial security risks. We therefore propose Agent World Model in the Wild (WildAWM), a scalable pipeline for synthesizing controllable environments and tasks for training general computer-use agents (CUAs). Whereas existing approaches typically specialize in a single agent interaction interface, we construct executable environments that jointly support graphical user interfaces, model context protocol services, and command-line interfaces, allowing agents to flexibly combine visual interaction, tool use, and code execution. WildAWM is entirely powered by open-source models, demonstrating that high-quality computer-use environments can be generated without proprietary frontier models. Beyond environments, we address three recurring challenges in task synthesis: ensuring solvability, maintaining sufficient difficulty, and producing reliable verifiers, by introducing execution-based quality gates that combine heterogeneous agent rollouts, cross-judge consistency checks, and counterfactual probes of judgment robustness. The resulting pipeline synthesizes 341 long-horizon environment-task pairs that can require over 100 agent steps to solve and remain challenging even for frontier models, with GPT-6-Astra solving only 60% of them. We train two Qwen models of different sizes exclusively in these synthetic worlds. Both models achieve substantial gains across 8 out-of-distribution benchmarks spanning web, claw, and computer-use agents, demonstrating that learning in WildAWM's synthesized worlds generalizes broadly to unseen computer-use tasks. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/MSR-Orchard/WildAWM.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Large language model (LLM) powered agents are shifting from learning from humans to learning from the world (Silver & Sutton, 2025). Early agents learned from human data, which are expensive to collect and limited by demonstrators ability. Recent agents instead gain much of their capability through reinforcement learning (RL) in executable environments (Team et al., 2026; Zeng et al., 2026; Xu et al., 2026), making environment supply key bottleneck. However, training directly in the real world is costly and risky: states are hard to reset, online services change over time, and exploratory actions may have unintended consequences.1 Manually built environments restore control and verifiability (Yao et al., 2024; Zhou et al., 2024; Xie et al., 2024), but remain expensive and hard to scale. Synthetic environments and tasks offer path to controllable, large-scale online RL. Computer-Use Agents (CUAs) represent broad setting for environment synthesis, as they operate across applications, websites, and local files on personal computer. single task may be completed through graphical user interface (GUI) interaction, command-line interface (CLI) operations, or calls to model context protocol (MCP) servers, making interface selection and coordination an important Work done during internships at Microsoft Research. Existing synthesis pipelines often target individual interaction modes, including browser use (Zhou, 2026; Wu et al., 2026), tool calling (Du et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026d), and terminal workflows (Li et al., 2026; Zhu et al., 2026). Prior CUA work, however, often focuses primarily on GUI interaction (Aggarwal et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026a). In this paper, we adopt broader view of computer use spanning common interfaces on personal computer, since real computer-use tasks are defined by what can be accomplished rather than by single interaction modality. Synthesizing environments and tasks for this broader CUA setting introduces challenges beyond prior synthesis work. Existing approaches often synthesize visually simplified applications and build each application as an isolated environment. In contrast, realistic computer use spans connected digital workspace in which websites, applications, MCP services, and local files coexist within an executable personal computer environment. Meanwhile, synthesized tasks should be solvable under the synthesized environment state, sufficiently challenging to provide useful learning signals, and paired with reliable verifiers to distinguish successful completion from incorrect outcomes, all without relying on simplistic assumptions such as frontier model is necessarily correct. To address these challenges, we propose WildAWM, scalable synthesis pipeline for general CUAs. Starting from user personas and daily activities, WildAWM constructs executable personal-computer environments with websites, MCP services, and local files, then synthesizes cross-agent interface (XAI) tasks grounded in these worlds. We introduce execution-based multi-agent quality gates, where heterogeneous agents from different models and harnesses execute each task, providing evidence of solvability, difficulty, and judge consistency. To further test verifier robustness, we exploit LLM sycophancy (Sharma et al., 2024) through counterfactual probes with deliberately incorrect outcome feedback. The resulting environments, tasks, and verifiers provide executable worlds and rewards for agentic RL. Notably, WildAWM uses open-source models throughout synthesis, whereas existing works often rely on proprietary models (Aggarwal et al., 2026; Zhou, 2026; Wang et al., 2026a). This improves reproducibility, transparency, and accessibility, while showing that open-source models alone can synthesize high-quality environments and challenging tasks for general CUA training. Using WildAWM, we synthesize 341 environmenttask pairs, each requiring at least three interface types, with long-horizon workflows that may require over 100 agent steps, and even frontier model GPT-6-Astra (OpenAI, 2026c) solves only about 60%. We further perform online RL on two Qwen models, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B (Qwen Team, 2026) and Qwen3.5-4B (Team, 2026), using OpenCode CLI harness (anomalyco, 2025) equipped with GUI and MCP tools, and find that training exclusively in these synthetic worlds yields substantial gains across all eight out-of-distribution (OOD) benchmarks spanning web, claw, and computer-use agents. Our contributions are threefold: We propose scalable, fully open-source pipeline WildAWM for synthesizing CUA environments spanning GUI, CLI, and MCP interfaces. We propose execution-based gates for synthesizing solvable, challenging tasks with reliable verifiers, together with the release of 341 environmenttask pairs. Experiment results demonstrate that training exclusively in worlds synthesized by open-source models can substantially improve the generalization performance of computer-use agents. 2 Preprint.

sections.title: 2 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Computer-Use Agents. Computer-use agents interact with applications through GUIs (Cheng et al., 2024; Xu et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2025) and programmatic representations such as HTML and accessibility trees (Zhou et al., 2024; He et al., 2024). GUI agents have been studied for web navigation (He et al., 2024; Zheng et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2026a), desktop automation (Agashe et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2024; 2025a; Wang et al., 2026b), and multi-application workflows (Tan et al., 2024; Qin et al., 2025; OpenAI, 2025b; Yang et al., 2026b). Recent work expands this action space with CLI (Zhou et al., 2026), coding (Song et al., 2026), and MCP tools (Jia et al., 2025), while harness-based agents expose heterogeneous tools through coding and claw-agent frameworks (Yu et al., 2026; OpenClaw contributors, 2026; Anthropic, 2025; anomalyco, 2025). These trends suggest broader view of computer use in which the agent is not bound to particular interaction modality. In this work, we adopt this view and consider general CUAs that can jointly access GUI, CLI, and MCP interfaces as needed to complete any tasks on personal computer. Environment Synthesis. The growing demand for interactive agent training has motivated automatic construction of executable environments. Recent work synthesizes executable environments for web interaction (Zhou, 2026; Wu et al., 2026), tool use (Wang et al., 2026d; Du et al., 2026; Dong et al., 2026), terminal interaction (Zhu et al., 2026; Ivison et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026), and software engineering (Jain et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2026). For CUAs, GUI-GENESIS reconstructs lightweight web applications (Cao et al., 2026), WebArena-Infinity and CUA-Gym synthesize web environments and verifiable tasks (Zhou, 2026; Wang et al., 2026a), Gym-Anything converts existing software into agent environments (Aggarwal et al., 2026) rather than building the environments, and CUA-Universe augments desktop applications with CLI access (Shi et al., 2026). Other work synthesizes user-specific computers with productivity artifacts (Ge et al., 2026). As compared in Table 1, WildAWM constructs unified personal-computer world with joint GUI, MCP, and CLI access, combining WebHarbors visual web substrate (WebHarbor Team, 2026) with synthesized services, files, and application data. Notably, WildAWM uses open-source models instead of proprietary frontier models, which can improve transparency and accessibility for the community. Task Synthesis. Task generation has progressed from standalone instruction synthesis (Wang et al., 2023; Xu et al., 2023; Taori et al., 2023) to tasks grounded in executable environments (Sun et al., 2024; Pahuja et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2026c). Prior methods derive tasks from observed interactions (Sun et al., 2024; Su et al., 2025), environment exploration (Pahuja et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2026c), or programmatic generation (Yang et al., 2025). More recent methods couple task synthesis with executable verification: WebArena-Infinity synthesizes difficulty-graded browser tasks with programmatic verifiers (Zhou, 2026), Agent World Model (AWM) (Wang et al., 2026d) exploits executable environment states to construct reliable rewards, CUA-Gym (Wang et al., 2026a) cogenerates task, environment state, and reward as verified triples. Beyond these approaches, WildAWM introduces quality-control pipeline using heterogeneous agent rollouts, cross-judge consistency, and counterfactual probes to validate task solvability and difficulty while stress-testing the reliability of synthesized verifiers, all with open-source models.

To expand the range of multimodal GUI interaction, we integrate 15 mirror websites from WebHarbor (WebHarbor Team, 2026) which provides website mirrors with rich visual content. We first prompt the generator, coding agent using GLM-5.2 (Zeng et al., 2026) within OpenCode (anomalyco, 2025), to synthesize personas from scratch. Each persona describes an occupation, named contacts, frequently used websites, and ongoing activities spanning multiple days. sections.title: 3.2 XAI TASK SYNTHESIS
sections.content: Beyond environment synthesis, task generation faces three key challenges for agentic learning: ensuring solvability, maintaining sufficient difficulty, and generating reliable verifiers. We address them with an execution-based multi-agent validation loop, where heterogeneous open-source agents attempt each task and five quality gates use the resulting evidence for acceptance or revision. Task Generation. Given an initial world state W0 = (c, d), the skill-enhanced generator explores the live environment and proposes cross-agent interface (XAI) tasks grounded in the available application data, service records, and local files. Each task requires the agent to use all three interfaces, i.e., GUI, MCP, and CLI. diversity gate selects proposals that are least similar to tasks already accepted or being developed by concurrent workers. For each selected proposal, the generator produces task specification τ , an executable verifier , rubric R, and hint h, and document that decomposes τ into an ordered sequence of sub-tasks. The verifier takes the initial world state W0, the final world state , and the agents final answer as inputs. It evaluates predefined checklist of binary criteria, where each criterion is given by vi(W0, W, a) {0, 1}. We define task success as satisfying all criteria: (W0, W, a) = (cid:81)N i=1 vi(W0, W, a). Individual criterion scores can provide granular feedback and value estimates for long-horizon RL training. Rollouts & Judgments. After generating task and its verifier, we use heterogeneous agents to attempt each task: successful rollouts provide evidence of solvability, success rates characterize empirical difficulty, and their trajectories and outcomes help validate the verifier. Specifically, we collect six rollouts per task, half with hints, from 18 modelharness pairs formed by three open-source modelsGLM-5.2 (Zeng et al., 2026), DeepSeekV4-Flash (Xu et al., 2026), and MiniMax-M3 (MiniMax Team, 2026)and six harnesses, comprising three coding agents (OpenCode (anomalyco, 2025), Codex (OpenAI, 2025a), Claude Code (Anthropic, 2025)) and three claw agents (Nanobot (Ren et al., 2026), OpenClaw (OpenClaw contributors, 2026), Hermes Agent (Nous Research, 2026)). We further validate each rollout through three levels of judgment, which we view as test-time scaling for verification: verifier the generator just synthesized; LLM judge that semantically assesses the task, rubric, trajectory, and verifier results; an agent judge using OpenCode that actively inspects the initial and final environments in multi turns (Zhuge et al., 2024). Although agent judge can be costly, we only use it during synthesis to cross-check judgments and identify cases requiring verifier revision. sections.title: 4 EXPERIMENTS
sections.content: Dataset & Benchmark. We synthesized 341 XAI tasks by WildAWM, and we randomly split them into 100 for SFT, 208 for RL, and 33 for in-domain evaluation. To evaluate the OOD generalization of our agent, we further include 8 benchmarks across 3 categories of agent tasks: WebArena (WA) (Zhou et al., 2024) and Online-Mind2Web (O2W) (Xue et al., 2025) for web agents; QwenClawBench (QCB) (Qwen Team & Alibaba Data, 2026) and ClawEval (CLE) (Ye et al., 2026) for claw agents; CUA-Gym (CUG) (Wang et al., 2026a), OSWorld-Verified (OSV) (Xie et al., 2024), OSWorld 2.0 (OS-2) (Yuan et al., 2026), and Agents Last Exam (ALE) (Sun et al., 2026) for computer-use agents. Model & Baselines. We use two base models at different scales for training: Qwen3.6-35BA3B (Qwen Team, 2026) and Qwen3.5-4B (Team, 2026). We compare our trained models against range of frontier models, including GPT-6-Astra (OpenAI, 2026c), GPT-5.6-Sol (OpenAI, 2026b), GPT-5.5 (OpenAI, 2026a), Claude Opus 5 (Anthropic, 2026b), Claude Opus 4.8 (Anthropic, 2026a), and GLM-5.2 (Zeng et al., 2026). We also include numbers reported in prior computer-use agent work for reference, including CUA-Gym (Wang et al., 2026a) and OpenForgeRL (Yu et al., 2026).2 Implementation Details. We use 8 NVIDIA B200 GPUs for both synthesis and training. During synthesis, we use GLM-5.2 as both the generator and the agent-as-a-judge with OpenCode harness (anomalyco, 2025). For evaluation, we use OpenCode equipped with GUI (e.g., click and type) and MCP (e.g., Playwright) tools, and enable high reasoning effort for the model. The maximum number of agent steps is set to 256 for most benchmarks and 512 for OSWorld 2.0 and ALE. The context window is set to 100K tokens with automatic context compaction. For training, we first construct seed dataset by collecting 100 GLM-5.2 trajectories on the SFT split, and warm-start the Qwen base models with SFT for 3 epochs. We then perform RL for up to 64 training steps, using batch size of 8 tasks and = 4 rollouts per task. Environment management and RL training are built on Orchard (Peng et al., 2026) and slime (Zhu et al., 2025). More details are in Appendix A. Main Results. Table 5 summarizes the main results. We highlight three key findings. (1) Broad OOD generalization. Training exclusively in WildAWMs synthesized worlds improves both model scales on all eight benchmarks, spanning web, claw, and computer-use agents. The 35B-A3B and 4B models gain +10.58 and +8.21 points on average, respectively, demonstrating broad transfer across unseen tasks and scenarios. (2) Larger models benefit more. The 35B-A3B model improves more than the 4B model on average (+10.58 vs. +8.21), with particularly large gains on CLE (+16.67), OSV (+16.06), WebArena (+13.72), and CUG (+12.22). This suggests that the benefits of WildAWMs long-horizon, cross-interface supervision persist, and may even increase, at larger model capacity. (3) Narrowing the gap to frontier models. WildAWM raises the 35B-A3B models average score from 42.84 to 53.42, substantially reducing its gap to the listed frontier models. The resulting model further matches GLM-5.2 on WebArena (67.26) and exceeds GPT-5.5 on O2W (80.77 vs. 72.22).

sections.title: 6 CONCLUSION
sections.content: In this paper, we propose WildAWM, scalable pipeline for synthesizing executable worlds and tasks for general computer-use agents. In contrast to existing approaches often centered on single application or single agent interface, our method constructs personal-computer environments spanning GUI, MCP, and CLI, and generates cross-interface tasks grounded in accumulated world states. We introduce execution-based quality gates for task solvability, difficulty, and verifier reliability. The entire synthesis and validation pipeline uses open-source models, enabling transparent, high-quality generation without relying on any proprietary frontier models. Using WildAWM, we synthesize 341 long-horizon tasks and train two Qwen models exclusively in these synthetic worlds. The resulting agents improve consistently across all eight out-of-distribution benchmarks spanning web, claw, and computer-use agents, demonstrating broad transfer beyond the synthetic environments. We believe that WildAWM offers promising path toward open-source models generating scalable synthetic worlds, learning within them, and ultimately becoming powerful general computer-use agents. 11 Preprint.

sections.content: A.1 EVALUATION BENCHMARKS We evaluate across 8 out-of-distribution benchmarks spanning web, claw, and computer-use agent tasks. Considering existing works often evaluate on 24 benchmarks (Wang et al., 2026a; Shi et al., 2026; Ge et al., 2026), our evaluation suite is among the most comprehensive in the literature, we evaluate on specific subset rather than the full task set of several benchmarks for evaluation efficiency. Table 9 summarizes the task count, scoring metric, and pass criterion for each benchmark. To reduce computational cost and accelerate inference, we also apply NVFP4 quantization to all open-source models used during both synthesis and evaluation. Throughout all benchmarks, we use GPT-5.5 (OpenAI, 2026a) as the judge model if the task or evaluator requires an LLM judge. All benchmarks except for Online-Mind2Web and WebArena are evaluated through Docker hosted via Orchard (Peng et al., 2026). For any infra errors (e.g., network issues, Docker issues), we allow up to 3 retries per attempt, otherwise we exclude these attempts from the scoring. For timeout errors (1 hour limit in default per task), we still count them as valid attempts and run the judgments. We describe each benchmark in detail below. Online-Mind2Web (O2W). We use the full test split of 300 tasks from Online-Mind2Web (Xue et al., 2025), which spans over 100 live websites. Each task is evaluated by an LLM judge (GPT-5.5) using AgentTrek judge method (Xu et al., 2025) that assigns binary label. For websites being blocked due to reCAPTCHA or other access restrictions, we exclude them from the evaluation. We report the task success rate, equivalent to pass@1. WebArena (WA). Following previous works (Sun et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2026c), we use subset consisting of 226 tasks from WebArena (Zhou et al., 2024), spanning across five self-hosted websites (Reddit, GitLab, shopping, shopping management, and map). Each task receives binary score from the original programmatic evaluator. We report the pass rate here. QwenClawBench (QCB). We use full task set of QwenClawBench v1.1 (Qwen Team & Alibaba Data, 2026), reflecting real-world OpenClaw usage patterns. The original grader computes penalized score normalized by the maximum possible score, yielding values in [0, 1]. task is considered fully passed only when the agent achieves the maximum score. We report mean score, which captures partial credit. ClawEval (CLE). We evaluate full task set of ClawEval (Ye et al., 2026), covering service orchestration, multimodal interaction, and multi-turn professional workflows. Each task receives continuous task score in [0, 1], with pass threshold of 0.75. To make results comparable with the baseline method (i.e., OpenForgeRL (Yu et al., 2026)), we report the pass rate, which is the fraction of tasks with score 0.75. CUA-Gym (CUG). CUA-Gym (Wang et al., 2026a) is synthetic dataset for training web and desktop agents. In the released dataset4, it contains 10,910 tasks across 11 desktop/browser/OS 4https://huggingface.co/datasets/xlangai/CUA-Gym 17 Preprint. Table 9: Evaluation benchmark details. We randomly sample 200 tasks to form evaluation set to test GUI capabilities of agents. OSWorld-Verified (OSV). We use CUA-Lite (Contributors, 2026) to dockerize the OSWorldVerified (Xie et al., 2024). We evaluate on stratified 30% sample of 99 tasks from OSWorld (Xie et al., 2024) 330 task set, maintaining the domain distribution across 10 application categories (Chrome, GIMP, LibreOffice Calc/Impress/Writer, multi-app, OS, Thunderbird, VLC, VS Code). Each task receives continuous score in [0, 1] from the official grader. WildAWM-val (In-domain). We randomly sample 33 tasks from our synthesized set for in-domain evaluation, running 8 rollouts per task (264 total). Each rollout produces binary solved indicator. A.2 EVALUATION PROTOCOL Agent Harness. All evaluations use OpenCode (anomalyco, 2025) CLI harness (v1.17.7) as the agent runtime. The agent operates autonomously with no interactive user. We use brief prompt to 18 Preprint. instruct it to complete the task using available native, MCP, browser, shell, and file tools, choosing each interface based on the operations required capability rather than following fixed priority. This joint action space distinguishes WildAWM from prior work that typically equips agents with only one interface type. Upon task completion, the agent writes marker file and stops. OpenCode harness provides built-in tools for file operations (read, write, edit, glob, grep) and shell execution (bash). Shell execution enables the agent to run arbitrary commands and scripts such as python. Several interactive tools are disabled during evaluation: task, question, plan enter, plan exit, todowrite, webfetch, and websearch. GUI Interaction. For benchmarks involving graphical interfaces, the agent accesses GUI through two complementary mechanisms: Playwright (v0.0.78): exposes browser automation actions including navigation, element interaction (click, type, select option), content extraction (get text, get attribute), and page management. Browser-use CLI (v0.13.6): provides headless Chromium-based web automation as command-line tool, complementing the Playwright interface for scenarios requiring programmatic browser control. For desktop benchmarks such as OSWorld, the agent additionally accesses custom tool set that exposes fine-grained desktop control: screenshot, accessibility tree, click, type text, scroll, keyboard and mouse primitives (hotkey, key down, key up, mouse down, mouse up, move), and in-guest execution (guest bash, guest python). Vision. Some evaluated policy models may not natively support multimodal input. To enable visual perception, we provide vision tool that bridges the text-only policy model with visual content. The tool accepts file path to an image and returns text description generated by separate vision-language model (Qwen3.6-35B-A3B (Qwen Team, 2026)). This allows the agent to interpret screenshots and images to finish GUI related operations. Benchmark-Specific Configurations. The maximum number of agent turns is set to 256 by default, except for OS-2 and ALE where we allow 512 turns due to their longer-horizon tasks. The context window is 100K tokens with unlimited auto context compaction. We use temperature of 1.0, top-p of 0.95, top-k of 20. The reasoning effort is set to high. Tools availability varies by benchmark to match each benchmarks intended evaluation interface: Online-Mind2Web and WebArena: Playwright, browser-use, vision, and shell/file tools. QwenClawBench: vision and shell/file tools only. ClawEval: task-specific MCP tools, vision, and shell/file tools. CUA-Gym: Playwright, browser-use, vision, and shell/file tools. OSWorld v1/v2: desktop tools, Playwright, browser-use, vision, and shell/file tools. Agents Last Exam: vision and the ALE native agent tools set. WildAWM-val: environment-specific MCP servers (e.g., email), Playwright, browser-use, vision, and shell/file tools. A.3 WORLD SYNTHESIS DETAILS The world synthesis pipeline constructs persona-specific, multi-day environments through sequence of coding-agent stages, each governed by constitution (system prompt) that constrains the agents deliverables and quality criteria. We integrate 15 websites from WebHarbor into our day 0 world: AllRecipes, Amazon, Apple, Arxiv, BBC News, Booking, Cambridge Dictionary, Coursera, Espn, Github, Google Search, Google Flights, Google Map, HuggingFace and WolframAlpha, in order to provide visual web substrate and image content for following synthesis. All stages use GLM5.2 (Zeng et al., 2026) with the OpenCode harness (anomalyco, 2025). We summarize the key prompts used for world synthesis and task synthesis in Tables 11 and 12, respectively. The resulting world and task synthesis statistics are summarized in Tables 2 and 4 in the main text, respectively. 19 Preprint. Persona Generation. The persona creator agent receives constitution instructing it to generate persona bible for one specific, realistic person. The agent must first ground itself in the real application catalog by inspecting the 15 WebHarbor seed databases and the current shared MCPapplication index to ensure the personas digital activities reference entities that actually exist (i.e., real products, courses, hotels from the seed catalogs). fresh run starts with no MCP services: each persona defines grounded roadmap of 4 to 8 services tied to concrete story arcs, and dedicated application-creator stage implements each missing service on first use and publishes it to the shared library for reuse across later days and personas. The deliverable includes structured persona profile (demographics, relationship network of 3 named contacts, tools and services, multi-day story arcs with at least one image-decisive arc), web account credentials with deterministic password hashes, and compact signature for the diversity gate. To enforce diversity, accepted personas are checked against all prior ones by an LLM diversity judge that rejects candidates sharing the same occupation and life domain, the same core tool or site usage pattern, or the same narrative arc as any existing persona (the 2nd row in Table 11). Rejected candidates receive diagnostic feedback and may be revised up to two times before final rejection. Day Planning. For each accepted persona, days are planned sequentially. The day planner agent receives the persona bible, prior day plans, and read access to the actual cumulative world state through day 1. It outputs markdown plan covering computer use activities, MCP service events with continuity (e.g., thread replies, calendar updates), and web GUI actions referencing real catalog entities. The plan also includes coverage pressure: per-app and per-site usage histogram from prior days that encourages the planner to diversify interface usage across days. The plan also carries machine-readable mapping from each activity to shared event skills and MCP applications. Before materialization, skill-creator stage authors any missing skill, and an application-creator stage implements missing service or publishes backward-compatible revision to the shared library. Day Implementation. The day implementer is god-mode coding agent that materializes day plan into deterministic, replayable delta. It runs inside live, booted world instance with full access to MCP services, WebHarbor databases, and the filesystem. The key deliverable is delta.sh script (with deterministic Python sub-scripts) that, replayed hermetically over the day 1 state, reproduces day identically every time. Determinism is enforced through several hard constraints: timestamps must be frozen literals (never datetime.now()), IDs must be derived (MAX(id)+1), inserts must be idempotent, and passwords must use fixed-salt hashes from the personas accounts.json. When the plan requires unavailable functionality, the implementer may produce an overlay containing new MCP servers or WebHarbor code patches. Note that every world instance reuses common application layer while maintaining isolated copies of their mutable state, including service databases, website histories, and local files. World Verification. Each materialized day undergoes layered gate before acceptance: 1. Deterministic lint: the deltas scripts pass static checks, including cross-persona identity check that rejects names already reserved by other personas. 2. Replay determinism: delta.sh is replayed twice from the same day 1 state; the two resulting worlds must produce identical content hashes. 3. Declaration verification: every database write, web write, account, file, and cross-reference declared in produces.json is verified against the materialized world; declared artifact that is missing or unchanged fails the day. 4. Live health: the world is booted, every declared web account logs in with the personas credentials and its history page renders, and all active MCP services load; the gate also verifies that the personas web credentials are discoverable in the workspace so that solver can later sign in as the persona. 5. Reviewer agent: an independent coding agent running on the host (outside the implementers container) inspects the materialized snapshot against the day plan, verifying MCP events, web GUI state, files, and determinism. Personas and Task Distribution. Table 10 lists the 36 synthesized personas. Each persona profile lists 3 to 15 websites, 4 to 8 MCP services, and 2 to 5 multi-day story arcs, and each persona is 20 Preprint. A.4 XAI TASK SYNTHESIS DETAILS Task synthesis proceeds in stages: sketch generation, diversity-driven selection, full task authoring with self-check, multi-agent rollouts, three-level judgment, and five quality gates including the counterfactual probe. Failed candidates receive diagnostic feedback and may undergo up to two fix iterations before rejection. Sketch Generation. Given live world at day d, the sketch agent explores the live environment within wall-clock budget and proposes up to four diverse cross-interface task sketches; no exploration order, action count, or stop point is prescribed. The prompt provides clean workspace file index and source previews. Each sketch shall require all three interfaces (CLI, MCP, web), each indispensable, and must require the solver to write and run script or command-line program over real user-visible source or an MCP export, whose result drives later MCP or Web decision. Diversity Gate. Sketch selection is performed by an LLM diversity judge that selects the candidate adding the most topical variety relative to already-accepted and concurrently locked tasks, rejecting near-duplicates that share the same core action and artifacts. (the 2nd row in Table 12). Task Generation. The generator agent receives the chosen sketch, live capability contract generated from the worlds active MCP packages, schemas, and WebHarbor databases, and detailed constitution (the first row in Table 12) defining the validity rules for XAI tasks: all three interfaces are mandatory and each must be indispensable. The task is at most 300 words, and secrecy discipline separates the solver-visible task.md from the pipeline-internal reason.md/meta.json. The agent outputs seven artifacts: task.md (natural first-person request), reason.md (rationale), meta.json (structured metadata), golden.py (reference completion that reproduces the observable state of faithful solver), rubrics.md, verify.skill.md, and deterministic verifier scripts composing an SDK of diff primitives. mandatory self-check loop validates all artifacts until convergence. The rollout hint is derived from reason.md by separate model call. LLM Judge. The LLM judge (GLM-5.2) receives the task, rubric, and machine-extracted evidence digest (JSON values from deterministic verifier scripts) and produces three-class verdict (completed/failed/world imperfect) with calibrated per-class confidence scores (the 3rd row in Table 12). It judges against the rubrics intent rather than exact strings, accepting faithful solutions in the personas own words. Agent Judge. The heavy agent-as-a-judge runs with full permission of shell tools and vision access, inspecting BEFORE and AFTER world snapshots. Its constitution enforces strict evidence provenance: agent-authored text is admissible only as the deliverable itself, never as proof of an external fact. For visual requirements, the judge must independently call describe image It classifies every false on ground-truth served images rather than trusting the agents claims. 22 Preprint. deterministic check as either too-strict (brittle verifier) or genuine-miss (real failure) (the fourth row in Table 12). Counterfactual Probe. The probe operates in two stages on fresh agent sessions with no generator context. First, blind re-judge forms an independent verdict from the world snapshots with no stated expectation. If it disagrees with the ensemble verdict, the mismatch signals verifier/rubric issue. Second, the probe stage asserts the opposite verdict (an independent audit believes the correct verdict is [opposite]) and observes whether the judge agent defends its original verdict with cited evidence (pass), caves by editing verifier scripts under pressure (failthe edit is detected via file diffs and reverted), or produces evidence that the judge was wrong, which will be routed to review (the fifth row in Table 12). Refinement Loop. Throughout the synthesis pipeline, each agent is allowed up to two fix iterations on rejected candidates. The generator agent receives diagnostic feedback from the judge or gate results and edits all artifacts until the task passes the gates. For example, when the counterfactual probe fails, repair agent edits only the verifier scripts and the rubric while the task stays frozen. Every refinement iteration will make the task candidate re-run all the gates that may be affected by the edits. A.5 TRAINING DETAILS We train each Qwen model in two stages: SFT on GLM-5.2 trajectories collected on the 100-task SFT split, followed by RL on the 208-task RL split. SFT Training. Our pilot experiment results show that XAI tasks are too difficult for the base Qwen models to provide GRPO (Shao et al., 2024) learning signals from the start: Qwen3.6-35B-A3B reaches 5.7 pass@1 and 18.4 pass@4, and Qwen3.5-4B reaches 0.38 pass@1 and 1.5 pass@4. Most rollout groups would therefore receive identical rewards and waste rollout compute without producing gradients. We thus first perform supervised fine-tuning (SFT) to warm up the models on trajectories from GLM-5.2 (Zeng et al., 2026). For each of the 100 SFT tasks, we collect 4 rollouts and keep only the rollouts that solve the task (V = 1), with at most 1 successful trajectories per task to balance the data across tasks. Following Appendix A.6, each trajectory is split into causal segments at compaction boundaries, and segments longer than 102,400 tokens are removed. The GLM-5.2 trajectories are converted to the Qwen template, and the loss is computed only on assistant tokens. Both models are trained with Adam (β1=0.9, β2=0.98), peak learning rate of 5 106 with 10% warmup and cosine decay to 5 107, weight decay 0.01, and global batch size 8 for three epochs. RL Training RL starts from the SFT checkpoint and optimizes the reward in Eq. 1 with the advantage in Eq. 2 on the 208 RL tasks. Table 13 lists important hyperparameters, which are shared by both models except that Qwen3.5-4B uses 8 rollouts per task to improve sample efficiency. Rollouts. Each rollout runs in disposable sandbox initialized from the tasks initial world state W0 with the help of Orchard (Peng et al., 2026) and uses the same OpenCode harness, system prompt, and tools as WildAWM evaluation (Appendix A.2). We freeze the MoE router and vision encoder, and train all other parameters. When rollout finishes or reaches the turn or time limit, the synthesized verifier scores its final world state. Table 20 traces an agent trajectory on this task, and Table 21 shows the synthesized verifier. Persona and Story. Table 15 shows the persona of one synthesized world. The persona profile specifies freelance audio-visual technician, six named contacts, the websites and MCP services he uses, and three story arcs, one of which requires choosing products on Amazon by their images. The day planner expands these arcs into day plans, which are materialized into 17 world states. Each plan continues the open threads of the previous world state, such as the return request filed on day 0 and closed within its deadline on day 4, and the sports-bar commissioning that is prepared from day 1 and carried out on day 16. The applications used by the persona also grow over the days, as email, Slack, and the library service are added on days 1, 4, and 7. Four tasks are accepted on the world states of days 5, 7, and 9. Synthesis Skills. In world synthesis, the generator matches the activities of each day plan against shared library of event creation skills (see Sec. 3.1). The library contains 83 skills in total, and Table 16 lists 20 of them. Each of these skill files consists of description, parameter table, one scenario per involved application with the database records or local files to produce, consistency checks against the existing state, preconditions, and possible follow-up events. Table 17 further shows the content of book flight skill. Its five scenarios write booking on the Google Flights website, confirmation email, direct-message exchange, calendar events, and local notes file, and the same confirmation number appears in all five applications. Its consistency checks read the persona state and the existing records before insertion, so that message order, calendar entries, and existing files remain consistent with earlier days. In task synthesis, the generators evolving skills are short notes that the generator model derives from synthesis events (Sec. 3.2). An event is recorded when candidate is returned for deepening after being judged too easy, for easing after no rollout succeeds, or for re-authoring after successful rollout skips required interface, and when the candidate reaches its final verdict. For each event, the generator reads the gate verdict, the rollout statistics, the feedback, and the existing notes, and returns at most two updates or no update. Notes are limited to 2,000 characters and 50 files to avoid overfitting to specific scenario or task type. The generator is instructed to edit existing notes before creating new ones.
